name: Dwifft
baseline: A naive diff implementation (README); today's default is the standard library's difference(from:)
verdict_reason: The README gives no numbers, only 'many orders of magnitude' faster than a naive implementation and 'almost certainly won't be the bottleneck'. In DifferenceKit's release build Dwifft 0.9 took 0.4732 s for 5,000 elements, 7.6x slower than the standard library's diff, and 187 s for 100,000, which would block a UI thread.
tier_reason: The library's own claim is directional with no numbers; the only measurements are third-party.
claimed_speedup: No numbers: 'considerably (many orders of magnitude) faster than a naïve implementation'. Third-party release build: 0.4732 s vs 0.0620 s for Swift.CollectionDifference at 5,000 elements, and 187.1341 s vs 5.0281 s at 100,000.
workload: Third-party check: arrays of UUID, 5,000 or 100,000 elements with deletions, insertions and a shuffled prefix (DifferenceKit benchmark).
hardware: iPhone 11 Pro simulator (host Mac not stated), for the third-party numbers
one_liner: LCS-based diff with UIKit bindings; claims speed with no numbers and measured 7.6x slower than the stdlib diff.
how_it_is_fast: Dwifft computes a longest common subsequence between the two arrays and turns it into insert and delete steps, with optimizations over a textbook LCS table. LCS needs work proportional to the product of both lengths in the worst case, so it scales poorly to large lists.
use_it_when: Small tables in existing code that already use its UIKit diff calculators
skip_it_when: Any list larger than a few hundred rows: 0.4732 s at 5,000 elements
You need moves: Dwifft emits only inserts and deletes
caveats: Third-party numbers were measured on the iOS simulator in 2019 with Swift 5.1.
The 149.6 s figure for Dwifft in DeepDiff's README is likely from a debug build and should not be cited.

evidence.quote: Dwifft is *fast* - a lot of time has been spent making Dwifft considerably (many orders of magnitude) faster than a naïve implementation. It almost certainly won't be the bottleneck in your UI code.
From 5,000 elements to 1,000 deleted, 1,000 inserted and 200 shuffled
From 100,000 elements to 10,000 deleted, 10,000 inserted and 2,000 shuffled
